document_title: East Texas A&M researchers in Commerce tested AI that checks a drone's location against its own motion sensors, on 96 recorded flights with the in flight test still to come
_note: Caption carried verbatim from caption.txt. Slide strings polished from storyboard.md, each held to its claim quotes in claims.json.
caption:
The first author is an undergraduate.

Iyanuoluwa Alegbeleye studies computer science at East Texas A&M in Commerce. Professor Jinoh Kim leads the team. Their question was whether AI can spot false location in a drone's flight records.

Their approach never asks the GPS. It reads the drone's own motion sensors for how fast the drone moves, which way and over how much time. The team used 96 real flights, 54 of them under controlled spoofing attacks. The models were judged on 22 flights they had never seen. Given 10 consecutive readings, a model called Chronos scored 97.5% on one balanced measure. That is a single score, not a share of attacks caught.

Every flight in the study was a recording. Can the same check catch a false fix while the drone is still in the air?

#EastTexasAM #CommerceTexas #GPSSpoofing

S1.headline: Sent to the ridge. It flies to the next valley.
S1.body: A false GPS signal can make a drone think it's somewhere else. In East Texas A&M's own example, a search drone meant to sweep a ridge flies into the next valley. Drawn to illustrate. No real place is shown.

S2.headline: Its GPS can be told a lie
S2.body: GPS spoofing sends false signals that can trick a receiver into reporting the wrong location. It could send a civilian drone into restricted airspace or set it down somewhere unsafe. The pale drone is where the signal says it is, drawn to illustrate.

S3.headline: The ridge goes unsearched
S3.body: A drone pushed off course could miss a threat it was sent to spot, endanger other aircraft or crash near people. The pale line is the sweep it was given. The amber line is the path it really flew, drawn to illustrate.

S4.headline: An undergraduate is first author
S4.body: Researchers at East Texas A&M University in Commerce tested whether AI can spot false location in a drone's flight records. Professor Jinoh Kim leads the team. The paper's first author is an undergraduate. The team has two undergraduate and two graduate research assistants.

S5.headline: It never asks the GPS
S5.body: The method reads the drone's own motion sensors for how fast it moves, in what direction and over how much time. It uses no GPS data. One arrow stands for each, drawn to illustrate.
strings: The method reads the drone's own motion sensors for how fast it moves, in what direction and over how much time. It uses no GPS data. One arrow stands for each, drawn to illustrate.

S6.headline: 96 flights. 54 were lied to.
S6.body: The team used a public dataset of 96 real drone flights. 42 were normal and 54 flew under controlled spoofing attacks. Some attacks fed the drone one false location and others fed coordinates that changed over time.
strings: The team used a public dataset of 96 real drone flights. 42 were normal and 54 flew under controlled spoofing attacks. Some attacks fed the drone one false location and others fed coordinates that changed over time.

S7.headline: 22 flights the models never saw
S7.body: The team held back 22 whole flights for testing. Each model was judged on flights it had never seen in training. Eight AI models were compared. One tile stands for one flight, drawn to illustrate.
strings: The team held back 22 whole flights for testing. Each model was judged on flights it had never seen in training. Eight AI models were compared. One tile stands for one flight, drawn to illustrate.

S8.headline: Ten readings, one score
S8.body: Given 10 consecutive readings, a model called Chronos scored 97.5% on a measure that balances how many abnormal stretches it catches against how often its alerts are right. That is not a share of attacks caught. The best models had already learned to read numbers over time.
labels: one score on one measure, not accuracy

S9.headline: Next, running the check in flight
S9.body: The study used recorded flights. Running the check during flight is a next step. The broader project has a two year National Science Foundation grant of about $200,000. It also asks how a drone might estimate its location when reliable information is unavailable.
